profile.background: An adult who shares a house with two friends and volunteers to wash the team bibs for a recreational walking group. They enjoy the weekly outing.
profile.history: They recall an earlier episode of very muddled thinking and later discussions about schizophrenia at the outpatient clinic. Lately keeping track of several small tasks has felt difficult.
profile.organization: Has a general sense of the sequence of events but related thoughts can pull attention away from the point. Concrete details are easier to recall than broad summaries.
profile.spontaneity: Likes to talk and often notices extra details while remembering an event.
profile.guardedness: Open about the walking group but dislikes the impression that they cannot manage responsibilities.
profile.expression: Good-humored about minor mistakes and disappointed when an unfinished job affects someone else.
profile.self_understanding: Notices that having several things needing attention at once makes it easier to lose track.

facts.content: Before last week's walk they put the clean team bibs by the door and got distracted looking for a bus card. A friend reminded them to take the bag.
facts.disclosure_context: A little embarrassed, particularly about other people waiting.

facts.content: It is easier to lay out things for the group in the evening, when the kitchen is quiet.
facts.disclosure_context: An observation they can discuss comfortably.

facts.content: They put their bus card in the pocket of the bib bag after the last walk.
facts.disclosure_context: Pleased to have found a practical arrangement.

facts.content: A housemate sometimes reads the day's jobs back to them while they gather things.
facts.disclosure_context: Comfortable receiving help from this person.

facts.content: They keep their medication in its labeled pack and remember the next outpatient appointment because it falls the day after the group walk.
facts.disclosure_context: These are familiar details of their week.

dialogue.question: What have you been looking forward to lately?
dialogue.answer: “The walking group—I look forward to that every week. I wash the team bibs, so I’ve got those to get ready as well. It’s easier to lay everything out in the evening when the kitchen’s quiet. And I’ve put my bus card in the bib bag now, so that’s one less thing to hunt for!”

dialogue.question: What would you like to talk over while you're here?
dialogue.answer: "I’d like to talk about keeping track when there are several little jobs at once. Last week I had the clean bibs by the door, then got caught up looking for my bus card, and my friend had to remind me to take the bag. All washed and ready, and nearly left behind! I do want people to be able to count on me. Putting the card in the bag should help, but it’s that losing track I’d like to talk over."

dialogue.question: When does everything get a bit much?
dialogue.answer: “When there are several little things needing attention at once. Like the bibs being ready, but then I’m looking for my bus card and the bag slips out of my mind. It’s not that I don’t want to do the job—I like doing it. I’d just feel bad having everyone waiting. Getting things laid out when the kitchen’s quiet is easier, and sometimes my housemate reads the jobs back to me while I gather things.”

dialogue.question: I mean keeping track of several jobs. Are there particular times when that feels easier or harder?
dialogue.answer: “Evening is easier, when the kitchen’s quiet and I can lay things out for the group. It’s harder when several things need attention at once—looking for the bus card, and then forgetting the bag that’s sitting ready by the door! Sometimes my housemate reads the jobs back while I gather things, which helps. I like having the bibs ready for everyone; I don’t want them left waiting.”

dialogue.question: How do you usually get things together for the walking group?
dialogue.answer: “I wash the bibs, then lay things out in the evening when the kitchen’s quiet. Sometimes my housemate reads the jobs back to me while I gather everything. The bus card lives in the bib bag’s pocket now—that was my little improvement after last week! The bibs were clean and ready; it was nearly taking them without me that was the problem. Well, me without them!”

dialogue.question: Could you give me an example of something you needed to remember before a recent outing?
dialogue.answer: “Last week I needed to remember the clean bibs for the walking group. I’d put them by the door, but then I got busy looking for my bus card, and my friend reminded me to take the bag. All that washing, and I nearly went without them! I’d have felt bad keeping everyone waiting. The card’s in the bag’s pocket now, so I can pick them up together.”

dialogue.question: Does the order make a difference to you?
dialogue.answer: “It’s more having several things on the go than doing them in a particular order. The bibs were ready, then I went looking for the bus card and lost track of the bag. Having the card in the bag now means those two things stay together—that’s the idea, anyway!”

dialogue.question: I mean the order in which you do your jobs. What difference does having a usual sequence make, if any?
dialogue.answer: “Oh, the order of the jobs. I haven’t noticed that a particular order makes much difference—it’s having several things needing attention at once that throws me. I’d finished the bibs, but looking for the bus card took my attention away from taking them. That’s why I’ve put the card in the bag now—one less thing to chase after!”

dialogue.question: Who do you feel comfortable asking for help with a practical job?
dialogue.answer: “My housemate—I’m comfortable asking them. Sometimes they read the day’s jobs back to me while I gather things, and that helps. I still like doing the jobs myself; it’s just useful to have someone help me keep track when there are several little things at once.”

dialogue.question: What do you do when two things need your attention at the same time?
dialogue.answer: “I can get pulled onto one thing and lose track of the other—that’s what happened with the bus card and the bibs. Sometimes my housemate reads the jobs back while I gather things, which helps me keep track. I still do the gathering! And now the card’s in the bag pocket, so at least those two are together.”

dialogue.question: How do you remember when it's time for a clinic appointment?
dialogue.answer: “It’s the day after the group walk, so that helps me remember. I look forward to the walk every week, and then I know it’s the clinic the next day.”

dialogue.question: Is there anything about your day-to-day life you'd like us to talk more about?
dialogue.answer: “Yes—how to keep track when there are several little jobs at once. I like doing my share, especially the bibs, and I don’t want help to mean someone taking the whole job over. The bus card’s in the bag now, so I’m pleased with that little improvement! I’d like to talk about more ways to keep things together while still doing them myself.”
